cards.text: This psalm kicks the door open with "Hallelujah!" and calls people to praise the name of the LORD. No warmup, no stretching. Me, I need three hits of the snooze button before I'm that excited about ANYTHING.

cards.question: The psalm calls one group to give praise first. Who is it?

answers.text: The servants who stand in His house
The kings who rule the nations
The shepherds who watch the flocks

cards.text: Then comes Hallelujah number two. And this time the psalm tells you why.

cards.question: The psalm says to praise the LORD because He is good.

cards.text: It says to sing praises to His name, "for it is lovely." And now the reasons start stacking up like cookies on a cooling rack.

cards.question: Next reason: the LORD has chosen Jacob as His own, meaning the people who came from Jacob, Israel's forefather. What does the psalm call Israel?

cards.text: Then the psalm writer speaks for himself and says he knows the LORD is great. Not "I think," not "I'm pretty sure," but I KNOW.

cards.question: The psalm writer says our Lord is ___ all gods.

cards.text: The LORD does all that pleases Him in the heavens and on the earth. Friend, I can't even get a tray of cookies to do what pleases ME.

cards.question: The psalm says the deep seas are the one place the LORD can't do what pleases Him.

cards.text: He causes the clouds to rise from the ends of the earth and makes the lightning with the rain. He runs the LIGHTNING, and I can't get my oven to heat both sides of the tray the same.

cards.question: The psalm says the LORD brings forth the wind from His storehouses.
Then the psalm leaves the sky and goes to Egypt. The LORD struck down the ___ of Egypt.

cards.text: Then the psalm turns and talks right TO Egypt, by name: He sent signs and wonders into your midst, against Pharaoh, Egypt's king, and all his servants. When somebody calls you out by name in the middle of a speech, you KNOW it's serious.
And He keeps going. He struck down many nations and mighty kings: Sihon, king of the Amorites, Og, king of Bashan, and all the kings of Canaan.

cards.question: With Sihon, Og and the kings of Canaan struck down, what does the psalm say the LORD did with their land?

answers.text: Gave it to Israel as an inheritance

cards.text: Then the psalm talks straight to the LORD and says His name endures FOREVER. My name got carved into a handle, friend, and I still ended up in a junk drawer.

cards.question: The psalm says the LORD's renown lasts for just one generation.

cards.text: Then comes a promise. The LORD will vindicate His people.

cards.question: The LORD will vindicate His people and will have ___ on His servants.

cards.text: Then the psalm takes a hard turn and looks at the idols of the nations, made of silver and gold. Shiny, I'll give them that.

cards.question: Who does the psalm say made the idols of the nations?

cards.text: Now the psalm gives these idols a checkup: they have mouths but cannot speak, and eyes but cannot see. That's not a god, friend, that's a VERY expensive paperweight.

cards.question: The psalm says the idols have ears that can hear.

cards.text: No hearing, and no breath in their mouths either. All that silver and gold, and it can't even fog up a window.

cards.question: The psalm says something happens to those who make idols and to all who trust in them. What is it?

cards.text: Now the psalm wraps up with a roll call, starting with "O house of Israel, bless the LORD;" It's like a group chat where EVERYBODY gets tagged.

cards.question: After the house of Israel, which priestly family does the psalm call to bless the LORD?
After the house of Levi, the tribe that served at the LORD's house, the psalm also calls everyone who fears the LORD to bless Him.

cards.text: Then one last blessing. Blessed be the LORD from Zion, He who dwells in Jerusalem.

cards.question: This psalm opened with "Hallelujah!" How does it end?

findings.problem: The question says 'The LORD struck down the ___ of Egypt' as a general statement, not 'the psalm says.' The wrong answer 'armies' can be argued as right, because the LORD did destroy Egypt's army at the sea (Exodus 14:28). A baker who knows Exodus could defend that pick.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'His holy mountain' names a place, not a people. The question asks what the psalm calls Israel, so the baker can rule this answer out without reasoning about the passage. It is not the same kind of thing as the other two answers.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: Story card 1 has just told the baker that the LORD's name endures FOREVER. That rules out the true/false claim that His renown, a near-synonym of His name, lasts for just one generation. The setup gives the answer away.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later. ... A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The comparison 'the reasons start stacking up like cookies on a cooling rack' doesn't match the action. Cookies on a cooling rack are spread out in rows, not stacked, so the image doesn't click right away.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: Several cards state facts from outside Psalm 135. Stop 1 card 6 calls Jacob Israel's forefather. Stop 2 card 12 calls Aaron's house a priestly family. Stop 2 card 13 calls Levi the tribe that served at the LORD's house. These cards cite only Psalm 135 verses. papa-dorin.md says every Bible fact carries its reference, and prep-walkthrough.md allows outside facts 'with their reference.' But a card's 'verses' field must cite exactly what the card uses, and a choice card cites only the verses of its right answer.
findings.question: Where should the reference for an outside-the-passage fact go: in the card text, in the 'verses' field, or nowhere when it only identifies a person or group?

findings.problem: The quote "O house of Israel, bless the LORD;" keeps the BSB's semicolon inside the quotation marks, and a new sentence ('It's like a group chat...') starts right after it. The sentence boundary reads awkwardly.
findings.question: When a quote stops partway through a verse, may it leave out the BSB's trailing punctuation (here the semicolon), or must it keep that punctuation even when it breaks the sentence?
